blocks.text: A national map needs a shared way to locate each feature. Early surveys often used district grids tied to local meridians and control. They worked for local administration, but adjoining districts did not automatically line up. Triangulation connected stations by observed angles; measured baselines supplied the scale. Surveyors built a wider positional framework well before computers could store it.

blocks.text: The Department of Lands and Survey also employed human computers. They reduced observations, solved trigonometric problems, adjusted networks and prepared coordinates for field and mapping staff. Rachel Gillanders appears in departmental records as a Computer and later in the New Zealand Gazette as a Draughtswoman and Computer in Christchurch.

blocks.text: Work on a national geodetic network intensified with the Wairarapa baseline in 1909. First-order triangulation extended across the country over the following decades. By 1950, the department reported completing its first-order fieldwork; the resulting control underpinned the New Zealand Geodetic Datum 1949 (NZGD49), a common reference for survey, mapping and engineering.

blocks.text: The network also served marine survey. In 1950 the Department of Lands and Survey reported supplying coordinates for 223 trig stations and other control to the survey vessel Lachlan for a coastal resurvey. The ship’s charting and the land survey were separate jobs, but the coastal positions depended on control established ashore.

blocks.text: Coordinate lists, observation books and adjustment calculations were already numerical models of place. Computers did not invent coordinates; they made it faster to reduce observations, adjust networks, transform positions and reuse the results.
